h: Wizards, oaths and the Radcliffe Camera
p: The Bodleian as we know it was founded by Sir Thomas Bodley, who reopened the university library in 1602 after it had been stripped and left in decline. Since then, it has grown into one of the great libraries of the world, and it's a legal deposit library, which means it's entitled to request a copy of every book published in the UK. Readers still make a formal declaration when they join, promising, among other things, not to bring fire or flame into the library.

Film fans will want to see the Divinity School, a 15th-century hall with an incredibly ornate vaulted ceiling. It appeared in the Harry Potter films as the Hogwarts hospital wing, and Duke Humfrey's Library, the oldest reading room, also stood in for the Hogwarts library. Both are often included on guided tours, though the exact rooms depend on which tour you book.

The circular Radcliffe Camera, with its dome rising above Radcliffe Square, is one of the most photographed buildings in Oxford. It's a working reading room, so you'll usually admire it from outside, but it's worth walking all the way round. Across Broad Street, the Weston Library is free to enter and hosts exhibitions and a treasures gallery, plus a café and shop.

Nearby, the Sheldonian Theatre, designed by Christopher Wren, and the Bridge of Sighs, linking two parts of Hertford College, are both within a minute's walk. Blackwell's on Broad Street is a book lover's paradise, and the tower of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin gives you a bird's-eye view over the whole scene.
